title: Education Efrat Furst When Prior Knowledge Helps, and When It Doesn't
author: Furst, Efrat
summary: Furst examines the 'prior knowledge paradox' -- the finding that prior knowledge strongly predicts future knowledge but does not reliably predict learning gains. Drawing on Simonsmeier's 2022 meta-analysis, Brod's 2021 commentary, and frameworks from Ambrose et al. and McNamara & McCarthy, Furst proposes a teacher-oriented sequence for understanding when prior knowledge helps or hinders. The central claim is that prior knowledge is not merely an asset but the actual material that new learning works with: new information only becomes meaningful when it binds in working memory with existing relevant knowledge. For this binding to succeed, prior knowledge must be active, relevant, accurate, and structurally coherent -- and Furst argues that structure (deep vs. shallow) should be assessed first because it dictates all other instructional decisions. The article offers a practical framework for teachers designing learning sequences, emphasising that every question about prior knowledge presupposes a clear learning goal.
points: * The 'prior knowledge paradox': meta-analysis shows prior knowledge can help, hinder, or have no effect on learning -- it is not a uniformly reliable asset, and the direction of its influence depends on whether it is active, relevant, accurate, and coherent. * Prior knowledge is not merely background context but the actual material of learning: new information becomes meaningful only when it binds in working memory with existing relevant knowledge -- gaps in prior knowledge produce gaps in comprehension, not just recall. * Teachers should assess the structure of prior knowledge first (shallow familiarity vs. deep, well-cemented schemas) before addressing activation or accuracy, because shallow knowledge misapplied can create harder-to-correct misconceptions than starting fresh. * Learning goals must be specified before any prior knowledge discussion is useful: relevancy, specificity, and accuracy cannot be evaluated except in relation to a target outcome, so instruction without a clear goal cannot use prior knowledge well. * Multiple converging research frameworks confirm that prior knowledge is a multi-dimensional variable -- not a simple on/off switch -- and teachers must address all dimensions.
quotes: While prior knowledge strongly predicts future knowledge, it does not necessarily predict knowledge gain (which measures learning). Looking deeper into the data they show a range of effects, some quite positive and some similarly strong but negative, and all the range in between. In other words, they show that prior knowledge can help, hinder or not change learning, and they call it 'the prior knowledge paradox.'
Prior knowledge is not just something that helps learning. It is the material that learning works with. New information becomes meaningful when it binds with something already stored in memory.
Only existing, relevant, active prior knowledge can bind with new information to create a meaningful construct.

Every discussion of prior knowledge is theoretical unless the desired outcome or goal is determined in advance. Notably, we cannot even talk about relevancy, specificity, and accuracy independently of the expected outcome.

As an analogy, we can say that flour is essential for baking. Yet it can also hinder the process if, for example, it is used without opening the package, used in the wrong amount, mixed improperly, or added at the wrong time.
Prior knowledge is essential for learning. When we learn, we process incoming information using whatever we have stored in memory -- our prior knowledge.
To build a pyramid or a conceptual understanding, we need to identify the elements and how they are organised: what's new and on what previous layer it builds.
